item.title: Highly capitalised stocks push gain to N2 trn in October
item.description: …As investors reap N4.5trn WoW By Peter Egwuatu The Nigerian stock market strengthened Month-on-Month (MoM), in October 2026, as renewed buying interest in heavyweight stocks lifted the benchmark of the Nigerian Exchange, NGX Index above the 250,000-point psychological threshold. The rally added N2.01 trillion to market capitalisation, reflecting strong price appreciation in selected large-capitalised stocks across the Industrial Goods, Financial Services and Energy sectors. According to analysts, although the market’s upward movement suggests renewed investor confidence, the uneven distribution of gains points to a selective investment strategy. Investors appear to be concentrating on stocks with significant market influence while maintaining a cautious approach towards other equities. This divergence between index performance and market breadth remains an important consideration in assessing the sustainability of the current rally. Specifically, breakdown of trading in October showed that the NGX market capitalisation closed at N165.114 trillion from 163.104 trillion in September. Similarly, the NGX All Share Index, ASI surged by 1.2% to close at 254,299.49 points from 251,211.67 points in September. Meanwhile on Week-on-Week, WoW the market gained N4.595 trillion as market capitalisation rose from N160.519 trillion the previous week in October to close at N165.114 trillion last week while the NGX ASI rose by 2.9% from 247,222.27 points previous week to close at 254,299.49 points last week. On the global market, the oil prices continued to record performance as the retreat in prices last week reflected a reassessment of geopolitical risks as diplomatic efforts sought to revive peace negotiations. However, analysts noted that the outlook for oil remains sensitive to developments in the region, and renewed escalation could quickly alter market expectations. item.title: Dangerous spices: How melted nylon additive keeps plantain chips crunchy
item.description: By Elizabet Adegbesan For some years, plantain chip has been one of Nigeria’s ultimate snacks which is affordable, accessible, and portable. But as inflation hovers at historic highs, a sinister economic survival tactic has crept into the informal food sector. Economy&Lifestyle discovered that to cut costs and keep chips crispy for days, some street entrepreneurs are turning to a dangerous additive: melted cellophane bags. The cost of a crunch The mathematics of running a small-scale food business in Nigeria today is brutal. The price of vegetable oil, cooking gas, and raw plantains has tripled over the last two years. For vendors like Halima Mohammed, who operates a roadside frying station, the pressure to maintain profit margins without raising prices is suffocating. “If I increase the price of a small pack from N200 to N400, the students will walk away. “People don’t have money. So, vendors look for shortcuts to make the oil last longer and keep the chips from getting soggy in humidity.” The “shortcut” involves tossing polyethylene plastic bags directly into the scalding oil. As the plastic melts, it blends with the vegetable oil, creating a glazing agent. When the plantain slices are fried in this mixture, they form a glassy, ultra-crisp outer shell. Crucially for vendors, the plastic coating prevents the chips from absorbing moisture, extending their shelf life from two days to over two weeks. A lifestyle of hustle and denial In the underbelly of Nigeria’s entrepreneurial ecosystem, the practice is an open secret, driven by sheer desperation. The lifestyle of a micro-entrepreneur in Nigeria is defined by any-way-raw-iron—a slang term for survival by any means necessary. With no safety nets and a failing grid that forces reliance on expensive petrol generators, the boundary between ethical business and hazardous malpractice has blurred. item.title: Monarch’s murder: Nwifuru seeks death penalty for kidnappers
item.description: By Jeff Agbodo Ebonyi State Government has forwarded an executive bill to the State House of Assembly seeking to make kidnapping a capital offence punishable by death without an option of alternative punishment. Governor Francis Nwifuru disclosed this at the weekend during the funeral of the slain traditional ruler of Ndufu-Alike autonomous community in Ikwo Local Government Area, HRH Eze Francis Igwe. Igwe, father of the immediate past Deputy Governor of Ebonyi State, Eric Igwe, was abducted on Sunday, March 1, while on his way to church. He was reportedly killed by his abductors a day after. Speaking at the funeral, conducted by the Assemblies of God Church, Nwifuru lamented what he described as the moral deterioration among Nigerian youths, expressing concern about their readiness to assume leadership positions in the future. He also pledged to implement any court decision against those arrested over the monarch’s murder, adding that the proposed legislation was intended to deter kidnapping and abduction in the state. The governor said: “I am worried about our present-day youths taking up leadership positions tomorrow. Some of our youths are not well informed, and they act so irrationally. “I am concerned because, with some of their attitudinal dispositions, there seems to be no future for our youths. “The youths need to have a rethink concerning certain actions of theirs, especially as concerns their attitudes towards community leaders. They should desist from treating their leaders as holders of their destinies.” He warned that the monarch’s murder should be the last such incident in Ikwo and other parts of the state. “I will not wait to execute the decision of the court over the murderers of this monarch, HRH Eze Francis Igwe. item.description: itel Energy, a clean energy and power solutions brand, has promised to repair or replace faulty solar power equipment within 48 hours for customers across Nigeria as part of its after-sales support. The company reemphasized their commitment during the Nigeria Energy exhibition week in Lagos, where it showcased new products and showed distributors, installers, both new and existing customers how its after-sales service works. The company said it offers remote services, home visits and product replacement where necessary. According to the company, after-sales service is an important consideration for households and businesses switching from petrol and diesel generators to solar power, because a faulty inverter or battery can disrupt electricity supply and business operations. He explained that customers needed assurance that equipment would be repaired or replaced when problems arose, rather than being left to deal with faults after purchase. “That trust comes from the type of equipment that we use and the promise of being able to replace or repair the assets when there’s a problem,” he said. Thomas also urged customers to look beyond warranty periods when choosing solar equipment, saying the speed and quality of support during the warranty period were equally important. “But even more important than that five-year warranty is what happens before the five years or during the five-year period. The company reemphasized their commitment during the Nigeria Energy exhibition week in Lagos, where it showcased new products and showed distributors, installers, both new and existing customers how its after-sales service works. The company said it offers remote services, home visits and product replacement where necessary. According to the company, after-sales service is an important consideration for households and businesses switching from petrol and diesel generators to solar power, because a faulty inverter or battery can disrupt electricity supply and business operations. Speaking on the sidelines at the exhibition, the Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of SunFi, a major distributor of itel Energy products, Rotimi Thomas, said the commitment boosted customers’ confidence in the products distributed through the company. “The 48-hour resolution commitment from itel Energy is very important for us as a distribution platform because we don’t make the product and when a consumer buys a product through SunFi, they’re actually really buying a trusted service,” Thomas said. He explained that customers needed assurance that equipment would be repaired or replaced when problems arose, rather than being left to deal with faults after purchase. “That trust comes from the type of equipment that we use and the promise of being able to replace or repair the assets when there’s a problem,” he said. Thomas also urged customers to look beyond warranty periods when choosing solar equipment, saying the speed and quality of support during the warranty period were equally important. “But even more important than that five-year warranty is what happens before the five years or during the five-year period. How do you respond when I report that I have a problem with the product now?” Thomas said the cost of solar systems remained a barrier to adoption, adding that the company offers instalment payment plans for households and businesses unable to pay the full amount. According to him, about 30 to 40 per cent of prospective customers still request payment plans, which shows the need for financing options that make clean energy more accessible. He said some customers preferred to pay between 10 and 30 per cent upfront and spread the balance over three, six, 12 or 24 months, or longer. Meanwhile, itel Energy’s Country Service Manager, Emmanuel Kumuyi, said most common complaints reported by customers included overloading, protection issues and incorrect installation. He said some problems arose when solar panels, inverters and batteries were not properly matched to the user’s power requirements. Kumuyi advised customers to use certified engineers for installation and to ensure that their systems were correctly configured. He explained that when a customer reports a fault, the company’s service agents document the complaint and refer it to an engineer for remote assistance. According to him, if the problem cannot be resolved remotely, an engineer is assigned to visit the customer’s premises. Where necessary, component or product replacement is initiated in line with the applicable warranty terms. The company’s National Distributor Manager, Lucky Ovenseri, said itel Energy had distribution coverage across Nigeria’s 36 states, with showrooms and dedicated energy after-sales centres in major cities, including Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Ibadan and Kano. He said the company also operated a replacement policy under which customers could receive another unit while their faulty equipment was being handled. At the exhibition, itel Energy showcased its newly launched PowerTank 1000 and IP54 11kW Hybrid Inverter, targeting customers with different electricity needs. The PowerTank 1000 demonstration featured a powered mini-chiller and a water dispenser, while visitors interested in the 11kW hybrid inverter sought information about pricing, installation, warranty coverage and its ability to support higher power demands. The company currently has 5 Flagship service centers, and over 200 service centers across more than 60 cities, backed by Carlcare and Transsion Group’s network of 2,000+ service centers spread across Sub-saharan Africa,Middle-East,and Asia. item.description: The naira’s exchange rate against the US dollar remains a major focus for businesses, importers, investors and Nigerians who depend on foreign currency for international transactions. The Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and the parallel market are two major segments of Nigeria’s foreign exchange market, with rates varying according to currency supply, demand and market conditions. As of Monday, November 2, 2026, the latest available figures indicate that the official NFEM rate stood at ₦1,346.26 per dollar, while the parallel market quoted the dollar at approximately ₦1,386.36. Official NFEM exchange rate Data published by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) showed that the naira traded at an average rate of ₦1,346.2565 per dollar on Friday, October 30, the latest available official trading data ahead of Monday’s session. The official market also recorded a closing rate of ₦1,346.00 per dollar, reflecting a marginal improvement from the previous trading session. The NFEM rate is determined by the volume-weighted average of transactions in the official foreign exchange market. It serves as the benchmark for official foreign currency transactions in Nigeria. This means Nigerians seeking to purchase one dollar from parallel market operators would need approximately ₦1,386, although the actual amount may vary depending on the dealer and location. The parallel market rates are indicative and may change throughout the day in response to foreign exchange demand and supply. Difference between official and parallel market rates The difference between the latest official NFEM weighted average of ₦1,346.26 and the parallel market selling rate of ₦1,386.36 is approximately ₦40.10 per dollar. The gap reflects differences in foreign exchange supply, demand and pricing across the two markets. For individuals and businesses purchasing dollars, the parallel market selling rate remains an important consideration, particularly for transactions that cannot be processed through official banking channels. How much is $100 in naira today? At the latest available official NFEM rate of ₦1,346.26, $100 is equivalent to approximately ₦134,626. At the parallel market selling rate of ₦1,386.36, $100 would cost approximately ₦138,636. These figures are indicative and do not necessarily represent the final rates offered by banks or individual currency dealers. Nigerians are advised to confirm prevailing exchange rates with their banks or licensed Bureau de Change operators before conducting foreign exchange transactions. item.title: OPEC+ holds December oil output steady to support market stability
item.description: By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as OPEC+, have agreed to maintain their September 2026 required production levels for December to support stability in the global oil market. The countries — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman — reached the agreement at a virtual meeting on November 1, 2026, where they reviewed “global market conditions and outlook”. The seven producers, which announced additional voluntary production adjustments in April and November 2023, decided to retain their existing production requirements for December. In a statement after the meeting, the countries reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation among oil-producing nations and stability in the international market. The statement read: “The seven participating countries decided to maintain September 2026 required production for December 2026.” The countries also reiterated their “collective commitment to achieve full conformity with the Declaration of Cooperation”, the framework guiding collaboration between OPEC members and participating non-OPEC oil producers. They added that they would continue to monitor developments in the global oil market through regular consultations. “The seven OPEC+ countries will continue to hold monthly meetings to review market conditions. The next meeting will be held on 29 November 2026,” the statement said. The seven countries’ combined required production level for December stands at 31.01 million barrels per day (bpd), according to the accompanying production schedule. Saudi Arabia has the highest required production level at 10.478 million bpd, followed by Russia with 9.949 million bpd and Iraq with 4.431 million bpd. Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman have required production levels of 2.676 million bpd, 1.628 million bpd, 1.007 million bpd and 841,000 bpd, respectively. Reacting to the development in an interview, an energy analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the decision could support international crude oil prices, with positive implications for Nigeria’s revenue and foreign exchange earnings. Miriki faults Dickson’s remarks Technical Adviser to the Bayelsa State Governor on General Duties, Miriki Ebikibina, described Dickson’s comment as unfortunate, urging the former governor to exercise restraint and uphold the dignity expected of a former chief executive of the state and a serving senator. item.title: 3 feared dead, 5 rescued as two-storey building collapses in Osun
item.description: By Shina Abubakar OSOGBO—THREE persons have been confirmed dead and five rescued alive after a two-storey commercial building under construction collapsed at Owode-Ede, in Ede North Local Government Area of Osun State. The incident occurred at Zone 8, Oke Alaafia Community, at about 11pm on Friday, prompting a rescue operation by the Federal Fire Service and other emergency responders. In a statement, the spokesperson for the Federal Fire Service, Osun State Command, DSF Ojo Omoyemi Olamide, said the command received a distress call through its emergency line at about 11:30pm and immediately mobilised personnel to the scene. She said the five rescued victims were taken to Idera Specialist Hospital, Ede, for urgent medical attention, while the three bodies recovered were handed over to the Nigeria Police Force, A Division, Ede. “The incident involved a two-storey shopping complex used for commercial purposes. The building consists of six shops on the upper floor, six shops on the middle floor and two stores on the ground floor, covering an area of about 50m by 100m. “Preliminary investigation reveals that structural defects and the use of substandard materials are suspected to be the cause of the collapse,” she stated. Olamide said the rescue operation was completed and personnel returned to the station at about 9:26am on Saturday. She added that the estimated property loss was N100 million, while property worth approximately N150 million was saved. The operation was conducted in collaboration with the Osun State Fire Service, Ede Station; the Nigeria Police Force, A Division, Ede; and personnel of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), Owode-Ede Division. item.title: Gunmen abduct Plateau varsity student, shoot another in Bokkos
item.description: By Golok Nanmwa JOS—GUNMEN suspected to be kidnappers have abducted a 100-level female student of Plateau State University (PLASU), Bokkos, and shot another person during an attack on an off-campus student residential area in Bokkos Local Government Area of Plateau State. The incidents occurred on Saturday at about 8:40pm, raising concerns over the safety of students living outside the university campus. A student, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed the abduction to journalists in Jos on Sunday, saying the victim had gone out with another female student when she was seized. “Yes, the student was taken away by the attackers last night, and we have not seen her since then. She lives off-campus, but I don’t know her personally,” the student said. He lamented the growing insecurity in the area and appealed to security agencies to ensure the safe rescue of the abducted student. A university staff member, who also spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to comment publicly, said the institution was aware of the incident. “The university is aware of a reported shooting incident in one of the off-campus student residential areas. This would be the second such incident in four weeks,” he said. “While the incident did not occur within the university campus, which remains our direct responsibility to secure, we are deeply concerned that any of our students living off-campus should face such threats to their safety,” he added. The staff member said the administration of Prof. Shadrack Best had made concerted efforts to provide safe on-campus accommodation for all students. “However, due to severe financial constraints, the university is currently only able to accommodate about 1,000 students in its dormitories,” he stated. “The university appreciates the support of its Visitor and Plateau State Governor, Barr. Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang, as well as the Tertiary Education Trust Fund, TETFund, for providing critical infrastructure at the institution,” he said. “The university will continue to engage relevant authorities to expand both accommodation and security for our nearly 20,000 students,” he added. Efforts to reach the Plateau State Police Command’s Public Relations Officer, SP Alfred Alabo, for comments were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report. item.title: How melted nylon additive keeps plantain chips crunchy
item.description: By Elizabeth Adegbesan For some years, plantain chip has been one of Nigeria’s ultimate snacks which is affordable, accessible, and portable. But as inflation hovers at historic highs, a sinister economic survival tactic has crept into the informal food sector. Read Also: NAFDAC secures five-year jail term for fake Goya oil manufacturer Economy&Lifestyle discovered that to cut costs and keep chips crispy for days, some street entrepreneurs are turning to a dangerous additive: melted cellophane bags. The cost of a crunch The mathematics of running a small-scale food business in Nigeria today is brutal. The price of vegetable oil, cooking gas, and raw plantains has tripled over the last two years. For vendors like Halima Mohammed, who operates a roadside frying station, the pressure to maintain profit margins without raising prices is suffocating. “If I increase the price of a small pack from N200 to N400, the students will walk away. “People don’t have money. So, vendors look for shortcuts to make the oil last longer and keep the chips from getting soggy in humidity.” The “shortcut” involves tossing polyethylene plastic bags directly into the scalding oil. As the plastic melts, it blends with the vegetable oil, creating a glazing agent. When the plantain slices are fried in this mixture, they form a glassy, ultra-crisp outer shell. Crucially for vendors, the plastic coating prevents the chips from absorbing moisture, extending their shelf life from two days to over two weeks. A lifestyle of hustle and denial In the underbelly of Nigeria’s entrepreneurial ecosystem, the practice is an open secret, driven by sheer desperation. The lifestyle of a micro-entrepreneur in Nigeria is defined by any-way-raw-iron—a slang term for survival by any means necessary. With no safety nets and a failing grid that forces reliance on expensive petrol generators, the boundary between ethical business and hazardous malpractice has blurred. Osaro Jimoh, a distributor who supplies packaged chips to traffic vendors on the , admitted that the market rewards the longest-lasting product. “The boys selling in traffic need chips that stay crunchy under the hot sun for days. If the chips go soft, the motorists will throw them back at us. Nobody asks how the crunch is made; they just want the crunch. “I don’t know the preservative used to achieve such crunchiness.” For the millions of consumers who rely on these cheap snacks to get through grueling multi-hour commutes, the lifestyle implications are passive but deadly. Plastic-infused oil releases carcinogenic compounds, heavy metals, and microplastics into the food, posing severe long-term risks to liver and kidney health. The regulatory blindspot Agencies have repeatedly warned the public against consuming street foods prepared with plastic additives. However, enforcing regulations in a vast, informal economy is nearly impossible. Millions of fryers operate out of residential backyards, unbranded and untraceable. Public health

item.title: Gully erosion destroys 30 houses, cuts off Edo communities
item.description: By Ozioruva Aliu BENIN CITY — No fewer than 30 houses have been destroyed by a ravaging gully erosion at Agor-Uwagboe community in Oredo Local Government Area of Edo State. The erosion has also cut off the community’s access road linking it with Ofumwengbe and Egbiri communities, leaving residents with limited means of movement. To ease the situation, residents have constructed a makeshift wooden bridge to enable motorcycles conveying passengers to cross the affected area. Residents of the community on Sunday staged a peaceful protest to draw the attention of the Edo State Government to their worsening situation. Speaking during the protest, a community member, Mr Ernest Uwagboe, said the gully was gradually extending into the community, threatening more homes and property. He warned that the entire community could be consumed by the erosion within three years if the state government failed to urgently intervene. The community’s spokesman, Kenneth Adoni, said residents had written several letters to relevant government agencies seeking assistance but had yet to receive any intervention. He appealed to Governor Monday Okpebholo to come to their aid, lamenting the hardship caused by the erosion. “We are begging Governor Monday Okpebholo to come and help us. For the past three years, the gully has caused lots of problems. We cannot cross to other communities. Whenever it rains, children cannot go to school,” he said. The residents called on the state government to urgently address the erosion menace and restore access to neighbouring communities to prevent further destruction and alleviate their hardship. item.description: By Nkiruka Nnorom, with agency report Leader of UK’s Conservative Party, Kemi Badenoch, has urged British not to apologise for its role in transatlantic slave trade, saying it would amount to a “navel-gazing distraction”, and would be used as lever for financial compensation by campaigners. Her comments came as UK’s PM, Andy Burnham, said he was considering a formal apology, before he flies to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda next week. Speaking to broadcasters yesterday, Badenoch described slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”. She also questioned whether it was worth future leaders attending the Commonwealth summit, given that it was now dominated by calls for reparations. In an article for the Guardian, Burnham said there would not be reparations in the form of financial compensation, but said he was prepared to engage in helping poorer countries restructure debt on more favourable terms. But reacting, Badenoch said leaders should be “honest about the whole history, not select the parts that are politically convenient today, especially given Britain’s leading role in ending the transatlantic slave trade”. She wrote in a social media post: “If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?” “On demands for reparations, whether through cash or debt relief, we have been down this track before,” she said. item.description: •Says fight against persecution must continue one year after CPC designation By Nkiruka Nnorom A member of United States House of Representatives, Riley Moore, has said Christians in Nigeria have continued to face unspeakable violence, one year after Nigeria was designated Country of Particular Concern, CPC. Moore stated this in a post on X to mark anniversary of designation of Nigeria as CPC by President Donald Trump. “Christians in Nigeria, and around the world, continue to face unspeakable violence. On this anniversary, we must rededicate our efforts to defend Christians in Nigeria and anywhere they face persecution,” Moore wrote. The lawmaker’s comment came as he reviewed impact of CPC designation, which he said was right decision by President Trump, alongside efforts by House Appropriations Republicans to condition aid to Nigeria and impose requirements to defend Christians, and advocacy by faith-based organisations. Moore said: “The President’s steadfast and decisive leadership, @houseappropsgop’s work to condition aid to Nigeria and impose requirements to defend Christians, and the tireless work of advocacy and faith based organizations has started to make a difference. “We saw the first Christmas without a massacre of Christians in recent memory. There is much more work to be done, but the government of Nigeria has shown signs of a willingness to address the violence against our brothers and sisters in Christ.” He had earlier noted that Nigeria witnessed first Christmas without massacre of Christians in recent memory, but said much more work needed to be done. An Okada man identified as Tasi’u, who attempted to escape, was reportedly shot and is currently receiving treatment at the IBB Specialist Hospital in Minna, the state capital. He said the teacher immediately instructed the pupils to return home while he also left on his motorcycle. “While on their way home, the pupils reportedly stopped at a borehole to wash their bodies and drink water. He said, “Currently, for about 14 to 19 days now, bandits have occupied some villages in Mariga, including Ragada, Maburya, Mazame, Kuimo and Kura, as well as villages in Rijau Local Government Area, which include Inana, Idaci, among others. “This situation has forced people to flee their homes for days. Just tonight, we received reports of an attempted new attack in Kuimo, which has forced the residents of that area to flee again in the middle of the night. As for the farms, they are truly in a critical state; if the soybeans and rice do not receive immediate attention and care, they will go to waste.” Recent abductions in Niger It has been 72 days since over 500 Worshippers were kidnapped from Juma’at mosques in Dekara and four other communities. Families said the abductors have yet to communicate with them since the incident. Terrorists had invaded four Juma’at mosques in Dekara, Gbezhin, Sabon-Gida and Kpenya simultaneously on August 21, 2026 and took away Worshippers. On 15 June bandits attacked farmlands in Pandogari District of Rafi LGA and killed one Dauda Galadima, a resident of the nearby Ruba village. They also abducted five farmers on their fields, including Nasiru Yakubu and his son, Bilyaminu. On July 24, gunmen raided Tashar Hajiya community in Niger State at about 2:30 a.m., killing one 25-year-old Mustafa Murtala and abducting three residents, one Alhaji Baza Baza, his wife and one of their daughters. On September 27, 47 farmers were abducted while harvesting groundnuts on their farms in Tugan-Rimi, Mariga LGA of the state. Daily Trust also recalls that on November 21, 2025, 230 pupils and students as well as staff members were kidnapped at St. Mary’s Primary and Secondary School in Papiri, Agwara LGA. The victims were later rescued through an operation coordinated by the Office of the National Security Adviser after several weeks in captivity. Also in November 2025, terrorists kidnapped an unspecified number of travellers along the Wawa–Luma Road in Borgu LGA, Niger State. According to a source, two passenger vehicles heading to Gupanti and Lumma communities were intercepted, and all occupants were abducted. However, farmers in Mariga, Borgu , Mashegu, Rijau told Daily Trust that attacks and kidnappings have become a daily occurrence. Forest security key to ending abductions – Experts A Senior Security Consultant, Auwal Bala Durumin Iya, has called on the federal government to strengthen security in Nigeria’s forests to address the persistent abduction of students, including Almajiri pupils and conventional schoolchildren. Durumin Iya, who is also a Quality and Internal Quality Assurance Manager of Homeland Security in Nigeria, said securing forests was critical to protecting rural communities and urban centres from kidnappers. He made the call while reacting to the reported abduction of some Almajiri pupils in Niger State while they were returning from their teacher’s farm. He said kidnappers deliberately targeted schoolchildren because their abduction attracted widespread public attention, putting pressure on governments and security agencies. According to him, the publicity generated by such incidents also creates fear among residents and could force communities to submit to the demands and directives of criminal groups. “When they kidnap students or Almajiri pupils, the attention of the public goes directly to that kidnapping, and they want wider publicity. When they get wider publicity, it means the students or community will put pressure on security personnel and the government. It also creates more fear in the community so that people may obey their orders, thereby distracting the government and security personnel,” he said. The security expert identified the establishment of a specialised forest security system, which he described as a forest marshal arrangement, as one of the measures needed to tackle the menace. He explained that the proposed forest marshals should be educated and properly trained personnel with the capacity to secure both thick and thin forests across the country. “When our forests become secure, our villages will also become secure. item.title: AI-Generated Photos: We Are Already Cleaning Up Our Register – INEC
item.description: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) says it has commenced the process of cleaning up its preliminary Register of Voters following the identification of records with suspected AI-generated photographs and other irregularities. The commission’s Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, said on Channels Television’s Sunday Politics that its Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS) had flagged 268 records for review. “What we are currently doing now is looking at all these 268 records that ABIS already flagged as AI-generated or even something of irregularities,” he said. Bayode explained that some people allegedly used their official credentials to create questionable profiles, exploiting a registration option designed for persons with disabilities who do not have complete fingers or have no fingers. According to him, the option, known as special registration, was used to deceive the system and was among the irregularities detected by ABIS. He said the commission had begun cleaning up the affected records. “Those that we have seen, we are cleaning up,” Bayode said. Bayode Lawrence However, he clarified that not every photograph enhanced with artificial intelligence would be removed, distinguishing between images generated entirely by AI and genuine photographs improved with AI tools on mobile phones. “Those that we know it is the AI on the phone that helped enhance their pictures, we can’t exclude such people because it was the AI on the phone that does that. Such people will still be on the register but those AI-generated, those photographs, all these will be removed. We are already looking at them,” he said. The controversy followed the publication of INEC’s preliminary Register of Voters online on October 26, after screenshots circulated on social media showing questionable photographs attached to voter records, including entries from parts of Edo State. The concerns also included allegations of duplicate entries and reports that names of deceased persons appeared on the register. In response, INEC said the online version was the same preliminary register displayed physically at Registration Areas nationwide from October 9 to 15. It explained that the publication did not reflect all the data-cleanup activities already in progress. The commission also said the register was not yet the final certified version and that the display, claims and objections exercise was designed to allow members of the public to identify inaccuracies and questionable entries before certification. INEC has said it will complete the necessary verification, adjudication and data-cleanup processes before certifying the final Register of Voters on December 15, 2026.
